name: Neelakandeswarar Temple, Tirumannippadikkarai
deity: Shiva as Neelakandeswarar (Padikkarai Nathar), with the goddess Amirthavalli
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine on the Kollidam, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
summary: Neelakandeswarar of Tirumannippadikkarai, the village now called Iluppaipattu, is a Paadal Petra Sthalam on the Kollidam sung by Sundarar, where tradition says the Pandavas worshipped five lingas and the goddess turned a poisoned pool into nectar.

sections.history: Tirumannippadikkarai, known today by the village name Iluppaipattu, lies on the southern bank of the Kollidam in the Chola country north of the Kaveri. Its old name carries the memory of the Manni, the river that once flowed here: Padikkarai means the bank or landing, and the shrine is spoken of as Pazha Mannippadikkarai, the old bank of the Manni. The saint Sundarar sang a hymn to the Lord of this place in the seventh-century Tevaram, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The present temple is a structural shrine shaped by the medieval patrons of the Tamil country and kept in worship ever since, though the founding dynasty is not firmly recorded.
sections.architecture: The temple stands in a quiet village setting near the Kollidam, entered through an eastern gateway into a modest Dravidian enclosure. Its most distinctive feature is the number of its shrines. Beyond the sanctum of Neelakandeswarar, where the Lord is worshipped as a linga, there are separate sanctums for Padikkarai Nathar and for three further lingas, so that five lingas are honoured within the complex, each in its own shrine. The goddess Amirthavalli has her own shrine, and the sacred tank, the Brahma Theertham, lies close to the temple. Local sources differ on small details of the gateway and the arrangement of the shrines, so the visitor is best served by walking the whole enclosure.
sections.legends: The legend of Tirumannippadikkarai belongs to the Pandavas. In their years of exile the five brothers came to this place and found no lingas to worship. They lit lamps with the oil of the iluppai, the mahua tree that gives the village its name, and meditated on the Lord, and in answer to their prayer Shiva gave each of them darshan as a linga, so that five lingas stand here today. A second tradition tells that Duryodhana poisoned the temple tank to harm the brothers. The goddess is said to have drawn the venom out and filled the water with nectar, and the Lord, as Neelakanta, the blue-throated one, is remembered as the one who swallows poison for the sake of his devotees. The pool has long been called the poison pond, and the goddess is honoured here as Amirthavalli, the vine of nectar.
sections.festivals: The principal festival is the ten-day Chithirai Brahmotsavam in April and May, when the deities are carried in procession through the village. Maha Shivaratri in February or March is kept with night-long worship, and Tirukarthikai in November or December fills the temple with lamps. Monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirumannippadikkarai rewards a patient visit to a village temple far from the pilgrim crowds. Come first to the sanctum of Neelakandeswarar, then walk from shrine to shrine to greet the five lingas the Pandavas are said to have worshipped, and pause at the goddess Amirthavalli and beside the old tank of the poison and the nectar. Devotees come for health and for the long life of those they love, and women in particular hold the goddess dear. The road runs through quiet fields along the Kollidam, and within the walls the temple keeps the stillness of a very old sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning from about 6:00 or 7:00 until late morning, and again from the afternoon until about 8:00 pm; sources differ slightly, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The village, known locally as Iluppaipattu (Eluppaippattu), lies on the southern bank of the Kollidam in Mayiladuthurai district, about 18 km from Mayiladuthurai and some 22 km from Sirkazhi. Mayiladuthurai Junction is the nearest major railway station, and buses run from Mayiladuthurai and Vaitheeswaran Koil. Ask for Eluppaippattu when seeking directions. Tiruchirappalli is the nearest major airport.
